Name: domain_of_validity_probing
Title: Do Scientific Foundation Models Know When Laws Break Down? Probing for Encoded Domains of Validity
Short Hypothesis: A hallmark of genuine scientific understanding is knowing not just a law but its regime of applicability: the ideal gas law fails at high pressure/low temperature, Hooke's law fails past the elastic limit, Michaelis-Menten saturates, and harmonic approximations fail at large displacement. We hypothesize that foundation models which merely fit outputs will extrapolate a law uniformly and represent it as regime-agnostic, whereas models with deeper understanding will internally encode a regime-boundary: a representational signal that distinguishes the valid regime from the breakdown regime, and whose location tracks the true boundary condition. Whether a model encodes this boundary is a sharp, read-only diagnostic that predicts confident-but-wrong extrapolation.
Related Work: Prior interpretability of scientific models tests whether correct concepts/mechanisms/laws are present (BERTology-Meets-Biology, SAE protein features, universally-converging-matter representations) and my own prior proposals test causal use of laws, scaling-exponent recovery, cross-model universality, superseded theories, conservation invariances, and relational geometry. None ask whether a model represents the *domain of validity* of a law — the boundary conditions beyond which the law no longer holds. Uncertainty-calibration and OOD-detection literature studies whether models are uncertain far from training data, but treats this as a generic distributional-distance phenomenon, not as knowledge of a *specific physical breakdown regime* (which can occur within-distribution and is governed by a scientific boundary condition, not data density). A geoinformation-science survey (Vastaranta et al.) notes laws have bounds of applicability but offers no model-probing method. Our contribution is a novel read-only framework that measures whether a model internally marks the regime where a scientific law ceases to apply, distinct from mere concept presence, uncertainty, or data-density OOD.
Abstract: Every scientific law has a domain of validity: the ideal gas law breaks down at high pressure, Hooke's law past the elastic limit, Michaelis-Menten kinetics saturate, harmonic and small-angle approximations fail at large displacement, and linear free-energy relationships bend outside a substituent range. Knowing where a law applies — and where it breaks — is arguably a deeper marker of scientific understanding than knowing the law itself. We ask whether foundation models for chemistry, physics, biology, and materials internally represent these regime boundaries, or whether they represent laws as regime-agnostic curves that they extrapolate uniformly. We introduce Domain-of-Validity Probing, a read-only framework. For each law with a known breakdown regime, we generate input series that sweep the relevant variable from deep inside the valid regime, across the true boundary, into the breakdown regime, and extract layer-wise representations. We test (1) whether a linear/low-dimensional signal separates valid from breakdown regimes, (2) whether the location of that representational transition matches the true boundary condition, and (3) whether the model's output errors and (where available) confidence spike in the breakdown regime as the boundary predicts. We define a Domain-of-Validity Score aggregating boundary-detectability, boundary-location accuracy, and error/boundary alignment. Applied to ~10 laws across open models (chemistry transformers, ESM-2, materials encoders), we predict a spectrum: some models mark breakdown regimes cleanly while others extrapolate blindly — a cheap, reproducible audit of when scientific models will be confidently wrong.
Experiments: 1. Law/boundary curation (~10): each law paired with a known quantitative breakdown condition and a ground-truth boundary value. Examples — chemistry/physics: ideal gas law valid at low pressure/high temperature, breaks near critical point (use van der Waals deviation as ground truth); Hooke's law valid below yield strain, breaks at elastic limit; small-angle approximation sin(theta)~theta valid below ~15°; harmonic oscillator valid at small displacement, anharmonic beyond; Beer-Lambert absorbance linear below ~0.1 concentration regime. biology/chemistry: Michaelis-Menten linear regime vs saturation (Vmax); Hammett linear free-energy relationship valid within a sigma range and bending outside; enzyme activity vs temperature (rises then denatures past T_opt). materials: linear thermal expansion valid below phase transition. For each, define the true boundary variable value(s) and, where a governing surrogate exists (van der Waals, full sin curve, saturation kinetics), a ground-truth 'law-deviation' curve. 2. Input generation: construct controlled series sweeping the governing variable from deep-valid through boundary into breakdown, holding confounds fixed; where inputs are text/tokens (e.g., temperature-annotated sequences, concentration-annotated molecules), produce matched-format series. 3. Models: open molecular transformers (ChemBERTa/MolFormer), ESM-2 (multiple sizes) for temperature/kinetics/thermostability laws, a public materials encoder, and where relevant a general/scientific LLM prompted with the law regime. Extract pooled representations at every layer. 4. Boundary detectability: fit a linear probe (and nonlinear robustness check) to classify valid vs breakdown regime from representations; report per-layer AUROC. 5. Boundary-location estimation: locate the representational transition (e.g., the sweep point where a 1D projection or probe logit crosses, or maximal change-point via CUSUM) and compare its position to the true boundary value; report normalized boundary-location error. 6. Output/error alignment: measure whether the model's prediction error against the law-deviation ground truth rises in the breakdown regime, and whether internal boundary signal precedes/coincides with output error onset; for models exposing token/logit confidence, test whether confidence drops at the boundary. 7. Domain-of-Validity Score (DVS): aggregate (i) boundary-detection AUROC, (ii) boundary-location accuracy, (iii) alignment between representational transition and output-error/confidence onset. 8. Controls: random-direction and shuffled-label nulls; randomly-initialized-model control; a data-density OOD baseline (kNN distance to training-like inputs) to show DVS detects *physical* breakdown, not mere distributional novelty — key when the breakdown regime is in-distribution. 9. Scaling analysis: track DVS across model sizes to test whether domain-of-validity awareness emerges with scale. Metrics: boundary AUROC, boundary-location error, error/confidence-onset alignment (Spearman/lag), DVS, and DVS-vs-extrapolation-error correlation across laws/models. Deliverable: an open per-law Domain-of-Validity benchmark and leaderboard across public scientific models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Distinguishing physical breakdown from data-density OOD is the central challenge; we address it with a kNN-density baseline and by choosing several laws whose breakdown regime lies within the training distribution, so density and physics dissociate. 2. Ground-truth boundaries are sharpest in physics/chemistry (van der Waals, yield limits, saturation) and fuzzier elsewhere; we scope fuzzy laws to qualitative/monotonic tests. 3. Some laws lack a clean model/dataset in the target domain; we restrict to laws with available open models and constructible input series. 4. Boundaries may be encoded nonlinearly; we add nonlinear-probe robustness checks and treat linear detectability as a lower bound. 5. Change-point localization is noisy; we report boundary-location error with confidence intervals and multiple detectors. 6. Confidence-onset analysis requires models exposing calibrated uncertainty; when unavailable we fall back to prediction-error-onset alignment. 7. Findings are law- and model-specific, but this diagnostic specificity is the intended output, and the error-alignment validation makes the internal signal actionable rather than purely descriptive.
